title: When a Business Can’t Afford It, Neither Should You
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder tackles a specific and uncomfortable question for owners running several companies: whether profits from a rising venture should be used to settle the debts of a failing one. Her answer is no, on the principle, borrowed from Daymond John, that if a company cannot afford something the owner should not be personally paying for it. The shoe store and laundromat analogy does the work of explaining separate entities, separate P&Ls and separate situations to people who see only that the owner has money. She describes the strange tension this creates for those who were part of the struggling business, and her husband's blunt formulation that the Bank of Mike and Summer is closed. A second strand covers partnership asymmetry, drawing on her own experience of being the only partner withholding pay and injecting personal cash while the other cited family obligations, and concludes that the imbalance is a red flag about the partnership rather than the business. She distinguishes investment with a path to return from what she calls life support. The piece closes by reframing the decision as honesty over people-pleasing, and notes it applies to employees trying to understand why hard calls get made.
points: The governing principle is stated as a boundary rather than a preference: an owner is not the business's emergency line of credit, and continual personal infusions are life support rather than leadership.
Mulder separates investment from rescue by asking whether there is a clear path to return, which gives owners a usable test for further funding.
Her partnership example turns asymmetric sacrifice into a diagnostic, arguing that one partner carrying both the company and the other's share of risk signals a broken partnership.
She anticipates the reputational cost directly, acknowledging that observers judge what they can see and will not credit the hundreds of thousands already poured in.
The closing distinction between care that is courageous and care that is careless gives the decision a moral frame rather than a purely financial one.
quotes: When one company is in free fall and another is on the rise, it creates a strange tension especially for the people who were part of the struggling business.
But that’s like asking your shoe store to cover the debts of your laundromat. Two separate entities.
Just because the owner has money doesn’t mean the business does. And when the business can’t sustain itself without constant personal cash infusions, that’s not leadership, that’s life support.
You can’t carry both the company and someone else’s share of the risk indefinitely. That’s not sustainability. That’s slow erosion.
But business isn’t about making everyone understand. It’s about making the right decision, at the right time, with the full picture in mind.
It’s not about a lack of care. It’s about the cost of care and knowing when that cost crosses the line from courageous… to careless.
And sometimes the most responsible thing you can do is walk away before it takes you under too.
